A 43-year-old man with a history of mild renal insufficiency and rheumatic heart disease is in the
cardiac care unit on postoperative day 5 after a mitral-valve replacement. He describes severe pain,
localized to the middle of his left foot, that started suddenly the previous night. His hospital course has
been complicated by mild volume overload for which he has received intravenous furosemide. He
reports no history of joint pain or recent trauma. He has a temperature of 38.2°C. He is in sinus rhythm
with a rate of 66 beats per minute, a blood pressure of 105/83 mm Hg, and an oxygen saturation of
94% while breathing ambient air. Physical examination reveals marked erythema and swelling over the
left midfoot but no swelling over the ankle joint. Squeezing the midfoot elicits severe pain even when an
effort is made to avoid the erythematous area. He does not have pain with plantar flexion or
dorsiflexion, but he cannot bear weight without substantial discomfort. Which one of the following
diagnoses is most likely in this case? Answer Choices: (A) Ischemic necrosis of the foot (B) Deep vein

thrombosis (C) Plantar fasciitis (D) Acute osteomyelitis (E) Septic arthritis (F) Cellulitis (G) Stress
fracture (H) Pseudogout (I) Cholesterol embolism (J) Gout
 A. Gout
B. Ischemic necrosis of the foot
C. Acute osteomyelitis
D. Deep vein thrombosis
E. Pseudogout
F. Cholesterol embolism
G. Cellulitis
H. Stress fracture
I. Septic arthritis
J. Plantar fasciitis
